11720: An outie is a type of belly button (also called a navel — the small mark on your stomach) that sticks outward, like a small bump or knob that pokes out from your skin.
Outie vs. Innie — understanding the contrast

Every person has a belly button, but not all belly buttons look the same. They fall into two types:

  • Innie — the belly button curves inward, forming a small pit or hollow. If you poke your finger toward it, it goes into the skin. This is by far the more common type.
  • Outie — the belly button curves or pushes outward, forming a small raised bump that protrudes out of the skin. It looks like a tiny knob sitting on your stomach.

Think of it this way: an innie is like a small bowl pressed into your stomach, while an outie is like a small pea or button sitting on top of it.

When a baby is born, it is connected to its mother through the umbilical cord — a tube that carries food and oxygen from the mother to the baby inside the womb. After birth, this cord is cut. The small leftover piece of cord dries up and naturally falls off within a few weeks, leaving behind the belly button.

How the skin heals and how much scar tissue forms at that spot determines whether the belly button becomes an innie or an outie. An outie simply means a bit more tissue built up during healing, causing that area to push outward instead of folding inward. It has nothing to do with how the cord was cut or tied — it's purely down to how the individual body healed.
Outies are quite rare. The vast majority of people — roughly 90% — have innies. Only about 10% of people (or fewer, by some estimates) have outies, making them noticeably less common.
Is an outie a medical concern?

In almost all cases, no — an outie is completely normal and harmless. It is simply a physical characteristic, like having a certain ear shape or nose shape.

However, in some cases, an outie is caused by a small umbilical hernia — a condition where a tiny bit of soft tissue from inside the abdomen pushes through a small gap in the abdominal muscles at the navel. This sounds alarming, but it is usually harmless. In babies, umbilical hernias almost always close on their own by age 3–4 without any treatment. In adults, if it causes discomfort or grows larger, a doctor may monitor it, though it rarely requires surgery.

So: an outie by itself is just a belly button variation. An outie caused by a hernia is still usually harmless, but worth knowing about.
Does it change with age or body changes?

Sometimes. Pregnant women often find that their innie temporarily becomes an outie as the belly expands and pushes the navel out. It usually returns to its original form after childbirth. Similarly, significant weight gain can sometimes cause a belly button to appear more outie-like, though this is not always permanent.
Any other notable use of "outie" as a noun?

Less commonly, in informal conversation, "outie" can refer to a person who is openly out about something — most often used in LGBTQ+ contexts to refer to someone who is openly out about their identity (as opposed to someone who is not). However, this usage is quite informal and niche. The belly button meaning is by far the most widely recognized and used sense of the noun "outie."

An outie is a belly button that protrudes outward as a small bump, rather than indenting inward. It forms based on how the skin healed after the umbilical cord fell off after birth. It's rare (only about 1 in 10 people have one), completely normal in the vast majority of cases, and carries no medical significance on its own. Its opposite is an innie, which is the far more common type of belly button.
11721:
"Outlandish" means so strange, bizarre, or different from what is normal that it almost feels like it doesn't belong in the real, familiar world. When something is outlandish, it hasn't just crossed the line of "a little unusual" — it has gone way past that line into the territory of "shockingly or absurdly strange."

Think of it this way: if someone shows up to a formal dinner in jeans, that's casual. If they show up in a slightly wacky printed shirt, that's quirky. But if they show up wearing a full suit of armor decorated with glitter and a six-foot feathered cape — that's outlandish.
The feeling and tone it carries

"Outlandish" is not a neutral word. It carries a quiet undertone of disbelief, amusement, or mild mockery — as if the thing being described has gone so far outside the bounds of what's expected that it's hard to take seriously. People hearing it often imagine something that makes them raise an eyebrow, laugh, or shake their head.

That said, in casual conversation, people sometimes use it with a kind of delighted admiration — "That outfit is absolutely outlandish, I love it!" — but even then, the core meaning stays the same: this thing is strikingly, dramatically strange.

It's a fairly strong word — much stronger than "unusual," "different," or "quirky." It sits in the same neighborhood as "bizarre" and "absurd," suggesting something that stands out in a dramatic, eye-catching, and often uncomfortable way. It's not the strongest English word for strangeness, but it's well above the middle.
What kinds of things can be described as outlandish?

The word is very flexible. It can describe appearance (an outlandish outfit, an outlandish hairstyle, an outlandish building design), ideas and claims (an outlandish theory, an outlandish excuse, an outlandish demand), behavior (outlandish conduct at a serious event), and stories or explanations that seem too far-fetched to believe.

The common thread in all cases is this: the thing being described feels so foreign to ordinary life that it almost seems like it came from another world.
How it compares to similar words

Strange/weird — These are more general and milder. "Outlandish" is more extreme and suggests something more dramatically, visibly, or conspicuously abnormal.

Bizarre — Very close in meaning to "outlandish." The main difference in feel is that "bizarre" can lean toward something that's mysteriously or unsettlingly strange (like a bizarre dream or a bizarre crime), while "outlandish" often focuses more on something that's visually striking or simply too far removed from normal life.

Eccentric — Usually describes a person's personality or habits, and is often used with affection. "Outlandish" can describe people too, but it focuses more on specific things — an outfit, a claim, an idea — and carries less warmth.

Absurd — Focuses on something being logically ridiculous or unreasonable. "Outlandish" is broader and focuses on general strangeness, not just logical failure.

Extravagant — Refers to excess in spending or decoration. It doesn't carry the sense of weirdness or alienness that "outlandish" does.

His outlandish theory that the moon was hollow and home to an ancient civilization made everyone in the room go quiet, then burst out laughing.

She arrived at the conservative office in an outlandish ensemble — neon yellow boots, a fur coat in July, and a hat shaped like a swan.

The villain's outlandish plan to hold the entire world's coffee supply hostage seemed more like a joke than a real threat.

Even by the wild standards of that reality show, his behavior was outlandish.

The new skyscraper's outlandish design — a building shaped like a giant tilted fork — divided the city sharply between those who loved it and those who were horrified.
When to use it vs. when not to

Use "outlandish" when something is so far outside the range of normal, expected, or acceptable that it genuinely shocks or amuses. If something is merely a little different or unconventional, reach for "unusual," "quirky," or "unconventional" instead. Reserve "outlandish" for moments when the strangeness is bold, dramatic, and hard to ignore.

One small thing to note: "outlandish" is slightly informal in register. You'd use it naturally in conversation, in articles, or in casual writing. It would feel slightly out of place in a very formal legal or scientific document — in those contexts, "highly unusual" or "extraordinary" would fit better.
11722:
An outlaw is a person who has broken the law and lives or operates outside the accepted rules of society — someone the legal system is looking for, or someone who openly defies and ignores the law as a way of life.

The simplest way to put it: an outlaw is a person who has put themselves beyond the reach of the law, whether by running from it or by refusing to submit to it at all.

The concept at the heart of this word is powerful. To be an outlaw isn't just to break a law once — it's to exist in a state of ongoing conflict with the law itself.

Historically, this was a formal legal condition. A person could be officially declared an outlaw by a court or authority. Once that happened, something significant changed: the law that normally protects every citizen no longer protected them. They lost their legal rights entirely. Society had, in a sense, expelled them. They were cast out — not just punished, but stripped of the shelter that laws provide to ordinary people.

Think of it this way: the law is like an umbrella that covers everyone in a society. An outlaw is someone who has been pushed out from under that umbrella — either they stepped out themselves, or they were pushed out — and now stands alone in the rain, unprotected and hunted.

In modern usage, the formal legal declaration no longer happens, but the spirit of the word survives perfectly. Today, we call someone an outlaw when they:

  • Are wanted by the law and actively evading authorities
  • Have committed serious crimes and are living on the run
  • Make a lifestyle out of crime, rather than committing one isolated act
  • Belong to a criminal group that operates outside the law (like outlaw biker gangs)

The key distinction from a plain "criminal" is this: a criminal is simply someone who has broken the law. An outlaw carries the extra weight of defiance and fugitive status. An outlaw isn't just someone who did something wrong — they are someone who has made themselves an enemy of the system and is living with the consequences of that.

Examples in sentences:

  • "The outlaw had been hiding in the wilderness for three years, one step ahead of the sheriff."
  • "Billy the Kid was one of the most notorious outlaws of the American frontier."
  • "The gang of outlaws terrorized the region for a decade before they were finally captured."
The Romantic Side of the Word

Here is something fascinating about "outlaw" that sets it apart from words like "criminal" or "thug": it carries a powerful romantic, rebellious image in culture — especially in American culture.

When people picture an outlaw, they often picture someone like a Wild West gunslinger, a Robin Hood figure, or a lone rebel who refused to be tamed by society. Outlaws like Jesse James, Bonnie and Clyde, and Billy the Kid became legends — not just criminals, but symbols of freedom, defiance, and living by your own rules. Even if we know they were dangerous and caused real harm, there's a certain fascination, even admiration, in how their stories are told.

Why? Because the outlaw represents something deeply appealing to the human imagination: the idea of someone who looked at society's rules, decided they weren't going to follow them, and took their chances. That reads as bold, wild, and free — even when it's also destructive.

This romantic image is so strong that the word "outlaw" is used in art, music, and storytelling to describe rebels with a heroic or sympathetic quality that the word "criminal" would never give.

Because of that rebellious image, "outlaw" has also slipped into informal, everyday speech to describe anyone who bends or breaks the rules — not necessarily a dangerous criminal, but someone who lives on their own terms and doesn't care much for authority or convention.

  • "He's always been a bit of an outlaw — he does things his own way and doesn't apologize for it."
  • "She's the outlaw of the family; she moved across the world and started her own business against everyone's advice."

In this softer sense, calling someone an outlaw is almost a compliment — it suggests they're independent, daring, and unapologetically themselves.

It helps to see how "outlaw" sits among related words:

Criminal — A broad, neutral word for anyone who commits a crime. No specific image attached. An outlaw is a type of criminal, but not every criminal is an outlaw. A person who commits tax fraud is a criminal; they probably aren't an outlaw.

Fugitive — Specifically someone fleeing from the law after a crime. A fugitive might be an ordinary person who panicked and ran. An outlaw suggests a deeper, more committed opposition to the law — a lifestyle, not just a flight response.

Bandit — A criminal who steals, often violently, typically in groups (think highway robbers or bandits ambushing travelers). It's narrower than outlaw.

Rebel — Someone who opposes authority or the system. A rebel may or may not break the law. An outlaw has definitely crossed into illegal territory.

The unique space that outlaw occupies: it combines serious criminal + fugitive status + defiant, independent spirit + romantic cultural weight. No other word does all of that at once.

An outlaw (noun) is a person who lives outside the law — either because they are a wanted criminal evading justice, or because they have chosen a life of crime and defiance as their way of being. The word carries a strong historical meaning (someone stripped of legal protection and hunted by society), a serious modern meaning (a criminal on the run or living a lawless life), and a softer, romantic meaning (a free-spirited rebel who refuses to be bound by rules). It is more vivid, dramatic, and culturally loaded than the plain word "criminal" — and that extra charge is precisely what makes it so widely used in storytelling, music, and everyday speech.
11723:
When someone outlaws something, they make it officially illegal — forbidden by law. It is what a government, court, or other authority does when they decide that a particular activity, practice, object, or behaviour must no longer be allowed, and they back that decision with the force of law.

The moment something is outlawed, doing it becomes a punishable offence. The thing moves from the legal world into the forbidden zone.

Only those with official power can truly outlaw something. This includes:

  • Governments and parliaments (passing new laws)
  • Courts (through rulings)
  • Regulatory bodies (through binding rules)

An ordinary person cannot "outlaw" something in the strict sense — they can forbid it in their own home or workplace, but that is not the same. The word carries the weight of formal, legal authority.

Almost anything: activities, substances, practices, organisations, or behaviours. Some real-world examples across history:

  • Countries have outlawed slavery — the practice of owning human beings became a crime.
  • Governments have outlawed certain drugs — manufacturing or selling them became illegal.
  • Cities have outlawed smoking in restaurants and public spaces.
  • Nations have outlawed child labour — employing children in factories became punishable.
  • Some regimes have outlawed political parties — joining or forming them became a criminal act.
What Changes After Something is Outlawed?

Before: the activity is legal, even if unpopular or considered wrong by many.

After: the same activity is a crime. Anyone who does it can be arrested, prosecuted, fined, or imprisoned. The law now actively works against that thing.

This is important: outlawing something does not make it physically impossible — people can still do it. It simply means the state will punish them for doing so.
How It Is Used in Sentences

Active voice (a subject does the outlawing):

  • "The government outlawed the use of lead paint in homes."
  • "Parliament outlawed discrimination based on religion."
  • "The international treaty outlaws the use of chemical weapons."

Passive voice (something has been outlawed):

  • "Child marriage has been outlawed in many countries."
  • "The drug was outlawed after studies showed it caused serious harm."
  • "That political party was outlawed by the military government."

Present tense:

  • "Several cities are moving to outlaw single-use plastics."

Notice that the word works smoothly in all tenses and both active and passive constructions.
The Subtle Difference from Similar Words

Understanding where outlaw sits among related words sharpens your grasp of it:

Forbid — can be used by anyone, even informally. A parent can forbid a child from watching TV. An employer can forbid casual dress. It does not require law.

Ban — slightly broader. A school can ban mobile phones; a country can ban a book. "Ban" is used both formally and informally, with or without legal backing.

Prohibit — formal and official, but can exist in rules and regulations that are not necessarily criminal law (e.g., a contract can prohibit something).

Criminalize — very close to outlaw, but specifically emphasises the act of turning something into a crime. "Outlawing" something and "criminalizing" something are often used interchangeably, but "criminalize" focuses sharply on the criminal-justice angle.

Outlaw — sits at the serious, formal, legal end. It strongly implies that official law-making authority has acted, and consequences (legal punishment) now follow for violations. It is decisive, final, and carries a sense of something being pushed entirely outside the boundaries of what is permitted.

In everyday speech, people sometimes use "outlaw" loosely, without meaning a literal law:

  • "If I had my way, I'd outlaw loud phone calls on trains."
  • "They should outlaw this kind of rude behaviour."

Here, the speaker does not literally mean they want a parliament to pass legislation. They mean: this should be completely forbidden; it should not be allowed to exist. This is a rhetorical or hyperbolic use — expressing strong disapproval by borrowing the weight of the word. Context always makes it clear whether someone means it literally (a law is being passed) or figuratively (strong personal opinion).

You may already know the noun: an outlaw is a criminal, a fugitive, someone who lives outside the law — famously, bandits and outlaws of the Wild West. The connection to the verb is direct and illuminating: when you outlaw something, you push it (and the people who do it) outside the law. Both the noun and the verb share the same root idea — the boundary of what is lawful, and what lies beyond it.
To outlaw something means for an authority with legal power to officially declare it illegal, so that anyone who does it becomes subject to punishment under the law.
11724:
An outlay is an amount of money that is spent or paid out for a specific purpose.

That's the heart of it. When you spend money on something — especially a significant or deliberate purchase — that money you spend is your outlay.

"The outlay for the new machinery was $15,000."
→ The company spent $15,000 on the machinery. That $15,000 is the outlay.
The Key Idea Behind the Word

Think of the word in two parts: "out" (money going out of your pocket or account) and "lay" (putting it down, committing it somewhere). So an outlay is money you deliberately put out for something.

It is not about money you receive. It is always about money leaving you — being spent, paid, or committed to a purpose.
What Makes "Outlay" Special (vs. Just Saying "Cost" or "Money Spent")

"Outlay" is not just a fancy word for "cost." It carries a specific emphasis: it stresses the act of spending from your side, rather than just the price tag of a thing.

  • The cost of a car is $20,000. → This is the price.
  • Your outlay on that car is $20,000. → This is your money going out the door.

The word highlights your financial commitment — the cash or funds you are parting with.

1. For planned, purposeful spending

Outlay is used when money is spent with intention — for a project, a business, an investment, or a major purchase. It rarely describes casual or trivial spending.

"The outlay for the building renovation came to $80,000."
"Her outlay on medical equipment for the clinic was considerable."

2. In business and finance contexts

This is where the word truly lives. Companies, governments, and investors use "outlay" constantly to talk about how much money is being committed to something.

"The government's outlay on public transport rose by 12% this year."
"Investors are worried about the high outlay required to enter this market."

3. For both large and small amounts

Though it sounds formal and serious, outlay can apply to any amount — big or small — as long as the spending is intentional.

"With a modest outlay of $50, you can set up a basic home garden."
"The total outlay for the space mission exceeded $2 billion."
The Single Most Common Phrase: "Initial Outlay"

By far, the most frequent use of this word is in the phrase "initial outlay."

This means the money you spend upfront, at the beginning, before you receive any benefit or return.

"The initial outlay for the franchise was high, but the business became profitable within two years."
"Starting a blog requires very little initial outlay — just a domain name and hosting."

Think of it like this: before a farmer earns any money from crops, they must first buy seeds, fertilizer, and tools. That upfront spending is the initial outlay. The profit comes later. The outlay comes first.

"Initial outlay" is especially important in investment and business thinking because it tells you how much you need to put in before you can get anything out.

Capital outlay — money spent on long-term physical things like buildings, machines, vehicles, or equipment (as opposed to day-to-day running costs).

"The factory's capital outlay this quarter included three new assembly machines."

Total outlay — the full, combined amount of money spent on something across all stages.

"Our total outlay on the project, including delays and extra materials, was $500,000."

Cash outlay — money paid directly in cash (as opposed to credit, loans, or other forms).

"The cash outlay required upfront was only $5,000; the rest was financed."

Financial outlay — used to emphasize that the outlay is specifically monetary (sometimes used to distinguish from other types of effort).

"The financial outlay was significant, but the team's time investment was even greater."

These words are close neighbors, and it's worth knowing exactly how they differ.

Outlay vs. Cost

"Cost" is the price of something — what it is worth in money terms. "Outlay" is what you actually spent. These are often the same number, but the perspective is different. "Cost" is about the thing. "Outlay" is about your spending.

"The cost of the software is $500." → Price tag.
"Our outlay on software this year was $500." → Our money went out.

Outlay vs. Expense

"Expense" is a broader, more everyday word. It can mean any cost — including recurring, ongoing ones like rent, salaries, or utility bills. "Outlay" tends to feel more like a defined, specific sum committed at one time, often upfront.

"Monthly expenses include rent and electricity." (ongoing, regular)
"The outlay for the new office fit-out was $30,000." (one-time, defined commitment)

That said, in formal writing, "outlay" can sometimes substitute for "expenditure" or even "expense" without much difference in meaning.

Outlay vs. Expenditure

These two are the closest pair. Both are formal words for money spent. "Expenditure" is slightly broader and more often used for total or accumulated spending (like a government's annual expenditure). "Outlay" often feels more focused on a specific act of spending or a defined sum.

"Government expenditure on defence." (broad, total)
"The outlay for the new aircraft was $200 million." (specific sum, specific purpose)

In practice, many writers use them interchangeably, and that is perfectly acceptable.

Outlay vs. Investment

An "investment" implies you expect to get something back — a return, a profit, a benefit over time. An "outlay" is simply money spent, with no implied promise of return. Every investment involves an outlay, but not every outlay is an investment.

"The $10,000 she spent on equipment was an investment that paid off." (expects return)
"The outlay of $10,000 was spent on equipment." (simply states money was spent)

"Outlay" is a moderately formal word. You will see it in:

  • Business reports and financial documents
  • News articles about economics or budgets
  • Formal conversations about money and planning
  • Academic writing in economics or finance

You would not typically say in casual conversation:

"My outlay at the grocery store was $60."

You'd more naturally say:

"I spent $60 at the grocery store."

But in a business or financial context, "outlay" fits perfectly and sounds natural and professional.
Quick Real-World Examples Across Different Contexts

Business:

"The startup's initial outlay covered office space, laptops, and software licenses."

Personal finance:

"Buying a house requires a significant outlay, including the down payment and legal fees."

Government:

"The government announced a $4 billion outlay for infrastructure repairs."

Healthcare:

"Patients face a large outlay when purchasing prescription medication without insurance."

Small scale:

"For a small outlay of $20, you can buy the materials to make your own candles."

Technology:

"The company reduced its outlay on IT by migrating to cloud-based services."
The One-Line Summary to Remember Forever

An outlay is money deliberately spent or paid out for a specific purpose — it is your money going out, especially in a planned or significant way.

Keep that in mind, and you will never misuse or misunderstand this word. Whether you see "initial outlay," "capital outlay," or simply "outlay," you now know exactly what it means and why it is the right word for the job.
11725:
An outlier is something — or someone — that stands far apart from everything else in a group. It does not fit the usual pattern. It is the odd one out, but in a more extreme, measurable, and meaningful sense than just being "a little different."

Think of it this way: if you lined up ten things that are mostly similar to each other, and one of them was dramatically, strikingly different from the rest, that one thing is the outlier.
The Two Main Worlds Where This Word Lives

The word "outlier" is used in two broad ways: in numbers and data, and in everyday life. Both meanings share the same core idea — something that falls way outside the normal range — but they apply it differently.

1. The Statistical / Data Meaning

This is the original and most precise meaning of the word.

In mathematics and science, when you collect a set of data points (numbers, measurements, observations), most of them tend to cluster around a central range. An outlier is a data point that falls so far away from that cluster that it seems to belong to a completely different world.

Example:
Imagine you measure the heights of 10 students in a classroom:

5'4", 5'5", 5'6", 5'3", 5'5", 5'7", 5'4", 5'6", 5'5", 6'9"

Nine students are clustered between 5'3" and 5'7". But the tenth student is 6'9". That person's height is an outlier — it is so far away from the rest of the data that it immediately stands out as exceptional and unusual.

The outlier is not necessarily "wrong" or a mistake. It is simply a real value that sits far outside the normal range.

Why it matters in data:
Outliers matter a lot in statistics because they can distort your understanding of the data. For instance, if you calculate the average height of those ten students, the one 6'9" student will pull the average upward, making the group seem taller than it really is. This is why statisticians always look for outliers — to decide whether to investigate them, explain them, or handle them carefully.

Outliers can appear because of:

  • A genuine, rare exception (a truly unusually tall person)
  • A measurement or recording error (someone accidentally wrote 6'9" instead of 5'9")
  • A fundamentally different subgroup hidden within your data

2. The General / Everyday Meaning

Over time, the word "outlier" crossed out of mathematics and into general everyday language. In this broader sense, it refers to a person, group, event, or thing that is markedly different from the norm in any area of life — not just in numbers.

Here, "outlier" captures the idea of something that defies the usual pattern, expectation, or standard of a group it technically belongs to.

Examples:

  • A child who learns to read fluently at age 2, when most children begin around age 5 or 6, is an outlier in child development.
  • A small family-run restaurant that gets a Michelin star in a city full of fancy high-budget restaurants is an outlier in the food industry.
  • A film made for $10,000 that earns $100 million at the box office is an outlier in the film business.
  • A country that has almost no crime despite being very poor is an outlier among nations.

In all these cases, the outlier is something real and valid — it's just strikingly, unusually different from what you'd expect when you look at the broader group.
The Key Qualities of an Outlier

For something to truly be called an outlier, it generally has these qualities:

It belongs to a group, but barely fits in.
An outlier is still part of the group being discussed. A 6'9" student is still a student. A $10,000 film is still a film. But within that group, it is dramatically different.

The difference is significant, not minor.
Being slightly different doesn't make you an outlier. If nine students are between 5'3" and 5'7" and one student is 5'8", that's not really an outlier — it's just on the taller end. An outlier is a dramatic departure from the pattern.

It is noticeable and often surprising.
Outliers catch your attention precisely because they break the pattern so sharply. When you see one, your instinct is to ask: Why is this so different?
Outliers Are Not Inherently Good or Bad

This is an important nuance. The word "outlier" is neutral by itself — it simply describes the position of something relative to a group. Whether being an outlier is good or bad depends entirely on the context.

  • A person who earns ten times more than everyone else in their profession is an outlier — in a positive direction.
  • A building that collapses while all similar buildings remain standing is an outlier — in a negative direction.
  • A data point that turns out to be a typo or measurement error is an outlier — in a meaningless, accidental direction.

The word carries no built-in judgment. It only tells you that something stands far apart from the rest.

Since you're learning, it helps to see how "outlier" compares to words you might confuse it with:

  • Exception — An exception is something that doesn't follow a rule. An outlier doesn't follow a pattern. These are close, but "exception" is more about rules and categories, while "outlier" is more about measurable distance from a norm.
  • Anomaly — An anomaly is something irregular or unexpected. An outlier is a type of anomaly, but "anomaly" is a broader word. An outlier specifically implies a measurable, significant distance from a central group. Not all anomalies are outliers.
  • Oddity — An oddity is something merely strange or quirky. It doesn't carry the sense of measurable distance from a pattern that "outlier" does. "Outlier" is more precise and serious in tone.
  • Extreme — An extreme is the furthest point on a scale. An outlier can be extreme, but not every extreme is an outlier. In a perfectly spread-out set of data, the highest and lowest values are "extremes" but might not be outliers if they're not dramatically separated from the rest.
A Sentence to Tie It All Together

If someone asked you to define "outlier" in one clear sentence, you could say:

An outlier is something or someone that falls so far outside the typical pattern of a group that it stands out as strikingly, significantly different from the rest.
One Last Thing: The Famous Cultural Use

The word "outlier" gained enormous popular recognition through its use to describe extraordinarily successful people whose achievements go so far beyond what is normal that their success seems almost impossible to explain through ordinary means alone. A person who masters a skill to a degree that almost no one else on Earth has achieved, or builds something that reshapes an entire industry, might be called a human outlier — someone whose results place them in a completely different statistical universe from everyone else in their field.

This cultural use is consistent with everything above: the person belongs to a group (musicians, athletes, scientists, entrepreneurs), but their outcomes are so far from the average that they fall completely outside the expected range.

That is the full picture of what "outlier" means — precisely, clearly, and completely.
11726: Picture yourself standing on a hilltop, looking out at the world ahead of you. You can see the landscape stretching into the distance — the terrain, the weather coming, what lies ahead. This single image is the heart of "outlook." Every meaning of this word is a variation of that act of looking out.
Meaning 1 — Your general attitude or way of seeing the world

This is the most common and important meaning. Your "outlook" is the mental lens through which you view life, situations, or the world. It's not what you think about one specific thing — it's your deep, ongoing, default way of approaching things.

Think of it as your internal weather setting. Some people wake up and the world feels full of possibility. Others see obstacles everywhere. That difference is a difference in outlook.

Important: Outlook is not the same as a mood (which is temporary) or an opinion (which is about one specific issue). Outlook is a stable, broader tendency — almost like a personality trait in how you interpret the world.

Examples:

  • "She has a cheerful outlook on life." — Her general attitude toward life is cheerful.
  • "Growing up poor gave him a different outlook on money." — His experiences shaped the lens through which he sees money.
  • "Despite his illness, he kept a positive outlook." — He maintained an optimistic mental attitude even while sick.
  • "Their outlook on education is very different from ours." — The way they think about and approach education differs greatly from how we do.
  • "Try to develop a broader outlook." — Try to become someone who looks at things from a wider perspective.

Common companions: a positive / negative / optimistic / pessimistic / narrow / broad / gloomy / cheerful / fresh outlook; outlook on life / on the world / on the future / on work.
Meaning 2 — What is expected to happen; prospects for the future

Here, "outlook" doesn't describe a person's attitude. It describes the expected state of something in the future — based on current signs, evidence, or trends. Think of it as a forward-looking assessment.

Going back to the hilltop image: you're not thinking about your attitude this time. Instead, you're scanning the horizon to read what's coming — dark clouds, clear skies, rough terrain ahead? That's this kind of outlook.

This meaning is common in news, business, medicine, weather, and formal writing.

Examples:

  • "The economic outlook for next year is uncertain." — Based on current evidence, the economy's future state is unclear.
  • "Doctors say her outlook is good." — Based on her condition, she is likely to recover well. (In medicine, "outlook" is the everyday version of the word "prognosis.")
  • "The weather outlook for the weekend shows heavy rain." — The forecast for the weekend expects heavy rain.
  • "The company's long-term outlook is promising." — The company's future prospects look good.
  • "The outlook for peace in the region remains bleak." — There is little expectation of peace there soon.

Common companions: a bright / bleak / promising / uncertain / gloomy / rosy / dim outlook; long-term / short-term outlook; economic / financial / political / weather / market / health outlook.
Meaning 3 — A physical place from which you look out

This is the most literal meaning and the least common in everyday speech. An "outlook" can be a physical location — usually an elevated spot — that gives you a wide, open view of the surrounding landscape.

Examples:

  • "The hikers reached the outlook at the top of the trail." — They arrived at a high point where they could see the landscape all around.
  • "From the outlook on the cliff, you can see three valleys." — From that high viewing point, three valleys are visible.

You'll encounter this meaning mostly in travel, geography, and nature contexts. Road signs in hilly or scenic areas often say "Scenic Outlook" — a spot to pull over and enjoy a wide view.

All three meanings share the same root idea: directing your sight outward, toward what lies ahead or around you.

  • In Meaning 1, your mind looks outward at the world — that's your attitude.
  • In Meaning 2, you look outward at the future — that's your expectation of what's coming.
  • In Meaning 3, you literally stand somewhere and look outward — that's the physical vantage point.

They're all the same act of looking out, just in different dimensions.

Outlook vs. opinion:
An opinion is what you think about one specific thing ("I think this policy is wrong"). An outlook is your broader, ongoing mental stance — a general tendency in how you see things ("He has a suspicious outlook").

Outlook vs. view (as perspective):
Very similar, but "view" usually means your position on a specific issue. "Outlook" is more general — it speaks to your overall mental approach, not just one position.

Outlook vs. forecast:
Both describe expectations for the future. But "forecast" is more precise and data-driven (a weather forecast, a sales forecast). "Outlook" is broader and more impressionistic — it describes the overall expected condition, not a specific prediction.

Outlook vs. perspective:
Very close in meaning when talking about attitudes. "Perspective" often suggests why someone thinks a certain way (based on their background or position). "Outlook" focuses more on what that attitude is — the tendency itself.

Outlook vs. mindset:
Both describe mental attitudes, but "mindset" is more about your belief system and mental habits (a growth mindset, a fixed mindset). "Outlook" is more about your emotional or evaluative lean — whether you tend to see things as hopeful, doomed, interesting, threatening, etc.

—What it means
Meaning 1Your general attitude or mental lens toward life or a topic
Meaning 2What is expected or likely to happen; future prospects
Meaning 3A physical elevated spot offering a wide view

Meanings 1 and 2 are the ones you'll encounter constantly. Meaning 3 is straightforward once you know it exists.
11727:
To outmaneuver someone means to gain an advantage over them by being smarter, more strategic, or more skillful in your actions — especially in a competitive or challenging situation.

When you outmaneuver someone, you don't just beat them by being stronger or more powerful. You beat them by moving cleverly — by thinking ahead, acting strategically, and leaving them in a position where they have fewer good options or no good options at all.

Think of it simply as: "to get the better of someone through skill and clever strategy."

The word carries two ideas inside it:

"Out-" means to surpass or do better than someone at something. Like "outrun" means to run faster than someone, "outmaneuver" means to maneuver better than someone.

"Maneuver" (as an action) means to move or act in a careful, planned, skillful way to reach a goal — especially in a situation where there are obstacles or opponents.

Put them together: to outmaneuver is to make smarter, more skillful moves than your opponent, so that you end up in a better position and they end up in a worse one.
Where and How It Is Used

This word works in many different situations:

In war and military strategy:
This is actually where the word feels most at home. A general outmaneuvers the enemy by moving troops into a position the enemy didn't anticipate — surrounding them, cutting off their supply lines, or attacking from an unexpected direction. The enemy suddenly finds themselves trapped or at a serious disadvantage, not because they lacked strength, but because they were outwitted strategically.

"The smaller army outmaneuvered the larger force by crossing the river at night and attacking from behind."

In sports:
A player or team outmaneuvers the opponent by positioning themselves cleverly, moving in a way the opponent cannot easily counter, or creating an opportunity that the opponent didn't see coming.

"The midfielder outmaneuvered two defenders and got a clear shot at goal."

In business and competition:
A company outmaneuvers a rival by making a strategic decision faster, entering a new market before the competitor, or making a move the rival has no good response to.

"The startup outmaneuvered its larger competitor by launching the product six months earlier."

In politics and negotiations:
A politician, lawyer, or negotiator outmaneuvers the other side by making a strategic move — presenting unexpected evidence, changing the terms of debate, or putting the opponent in a position where every available response is unfavorable.

"The defense lawyer outmaneuvered the prosecution by introducing documents that completely shifted the narrative."

In everyday life:
You can even use it in casual, everyday situations where someone cleverly gets the upper hand.

"She outmaneuvered her brother and got the last slice of cake before he could reach it." (informal/playful use)
What Makes It Special — The Nuances

Understanding these finer points will give you a complete grasp of the word:

1. It's about cleverness, not just force.
If you overpower someone through sheer strength, that's not outmaneuvering. Outmaneuvering implies skill, strategy, and intelligent action. The person who outmaneuvers is usually the one who thinks more steps ahead.

2. It implies the opponent is left with bad options.
The result of being outmaneuvered is that you find yourself stuck — cornered, surprised, or in a position where you can't respond effectively. The person who outmaneuvered you planned for this. They didn't just get lucky.

3. It often involves an element of surprise or anticipation.
Outmaneuvering frequently means doing something the opponent didn't predict, or predicting what they would do and acting before they could. It rewards foresight.

4. It is almost always used in a competitive context.
There is always an opponent — a person, team, company, army, or rival — being outmaneuvered. You don't outmaneuver a mountain or the weather; you outmaneuver someone.

5. The outcome is a shift in advantage.
Before the outmaneuvering, both sides may have been equal — or the side that was outmaneuvered may have even been stronger. After the outmaneuvering, the strategic balance has clearly shifted. The person who was outmaneuvered is now at a disadvantage.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Several words are close in meaning, but each has a slightly different flavor:

  • Outsmart / Outwit — These focus purely on intelligence. You beat someone because you were mentally sharper. Outmaneuver can involve intelligence, but it specifically emphasizes strategic action and movement, not just thinking.
  • Outfox — This leans toward cunning and trickery. Outfox suggests you were sly, like a fox. Outmaneuver is broader and more neutral — it doesn't imply trickery, just superior strategy.
  • Outflank — This is more specific. It literally means to get around the side (flank) of an opponent, especially militarily. Outmaneuver is the broader, more general version of this.
  • Get the better of — A casual phrase with a similar meaning, but "outmaneuver" sounds more formal and specifically implies strategic action.

To outmaneuver = to defeat, outsmart, or gain a decisive advantage over an opponent through clever, skillful, and strategic action — leaving them in a weaker or more difficult position as a result.

It's the word you reach for when someone doesn't just win — they win because they were strategically smarter and made moves the other side couldn't anticipate or counter.
11728:
When something is outmoded, it means it is no longer suitable for the present time because something better, newer, or more fitting has replaced it.

The key idea is this: the thing being described was once normal, useful, or accepted — but time moved on, and it got left behind.

Think of it as something that has been pushed out by the modern world.

Imagine a typewriter sitting in the corner of a modern office. Everyone around it uses laptops. The typewriter still works — it isn't broken — but nobody uses it anymore because computers do the same job far better and faster. The typewriter is outmoded.

Now notice something important: you are not saying the typewriter was always useless. It was perfectly fine for its time. But its time has passed. That passing of time — and the arrival of something better — is exactly what "outmoded" captures.

Almost anything can be outmoded. Here are the main categories:

1. Technology and tools
When newer versions of something make older ones unnecessary.

  • "The fax machine has become an outmoded piece of office equipment."
  • "That outmoded software can no longer run on modern computers."

2. Ideas and beliefs
When a way of thinking was once widely accepted but is now considered wrong, harmful, or simply out of step with modern understanding.

  • "The idea that women shouldn't pursue careers is an outmoded belief."
  • "His outmoded views on education made him unpopular with younger teachers."

3. Methods and practices
When a way of doing something has been replaced by a better process.

  • "Bloodletting was an outmoded medical practice that doctors once used seriously."
  • "Their outmoded hiring process involved paper applications and weeks of waiting."

4. Fashion and style
When a look or trend that was once popular is now considered old and unfashionable.

  • "She arrived wearing an outmoded hairstyle that no one had seen since the 1980s."

"Outmoded" is a mildly negative word. When you call something outmoded, you are subtly criticizing it — suggesting that whoever is still using it or believing it has not kept up with the times.

It is not a harsh insult, but it does carry a tone of mild disapproval or pity, like saying: "This belongs to the past, yet it's still here."

For example:

  • "The company's outmoded management style was driving talented employees away."

Here, the word signals that the management style is not just old — it is a problem because it doesn't fit the modern workplace.
The Subtle Difference: "Was Fine, But Not Anymore"

This is the most important nuance to truly understand "outmoded":

It does not mean something was always bad.
It does not mean something is broken or defective.
It does mean something was once appropriate — but circumstances, time, or progress have made it no longer suitable.

This is what separates "outmoded" from just saying something is "bad." You are specifically saying: "The world moved forward, and this did not."
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding how "outmoded" sits alongside related words will sharpen your grasp of it:

Outdated — The closest synonym. Nearly interchangeable with "outmoded," though "outdated" is more commonly used in everyday speech. "Outmoded" feels slightly more formal and deliberate.

Obsolete — Stronger than "outmoded." When something is obsolete, it is completely no longer in use — it has been entirely abandoned. Something outmoded might still be in use by some people; something obsolete is virtually gone. A fax machine might be outmoded, but a horse-drawn plow in a modern city is obsolete.

Old-fashioned — More focused on style, manners, or social customs than on usefulness or function. Also less critical in tone — sometimes even affectionate. Your grandmother's recipes might be called "old-fashioned" fondly, but rarely "outmoded."

Antiquated — Suggests something feels ancient, almost from a distant era. It is stronger and more dramatic than "outmoded."

Archaic — The most extreme of the group. Means something belongs to a very ancient time, like a word or law from centuries ago. Much stronger than "outmoded."

So the scale roughly looks like this, from mildest to strongest:

Old-fashioned → Outdated ≈ Outmoded → Antiquated → Obsolete → Archaic
The opposite of outmoded would be words like modern, current, up-to-date, contemporary, cutting-edge, or relevant — all suggesting something that fits well with the present time.

• "The law was written in 1920 and is completely outmoded — it makes no sense in today's world."
  • "He clung to outmoded ideas about gender roles that made his colleagues uncomfortable."
  • "The factory replaced its outmoded machinery with a fully automated system."
  • "Critics argued that the exam format was outmoded and failed to test real-world skills."
  • "Her outmoded phone couldn't run any of the new apps."

If you had to sum up "outmoded" in one sentence:

Something that was once perfectly normal or useful, but has been left behind by time and progress — making it no longer appropriate or relevant today.
11729:
To outpace something or someone means to move, grow, or progress at a faster rate than them — and to keep doing so over time.

Think of the word in two parts:

  • Pace = the speed or rate at which something moves or happens
  • Out- = doing something more than, or better than, the other person/thing

Put them together: to outpace = to maintain a faster pace than someone or something else.

Imagine two runners on a track. Runner A starts covering ground faster than Runner B and keeps pulling ahead. Runner A is outpacing Runner B.

Notice: it's not just that A is ahead at one moment — it's that A is continuing to move faster, which means the gap between them keeps growing.

This is the heart of the word: not just being ahead, but consistently moving at a greater speed, so the distance between the two keeps widening.
The Bigger Picture (Figurative Use — Where the Word Really Lives)

In everyday writing and speech, "outpace" is almost never about actual running. It's used to describe anything that grows, increases, or progresses faster than something else. The "pace" can be the pace of growth, change, production, demand, technology — anything measurable over time.

Some examples:

  • Demand outpaces supply → People want products faster than companies can make them. The gap keeps growing.
  • Prices outpace wages → Prices rise faster than people's salaries. Over time, people can afford less and less.
  • Technology outpaces regulation → New technology develops faster than governments can make rules to control it.
  • A startup outpaces its rivals → The startup grows and expands faster than its competitors.
  • A student's curiosity outpaces the curriculum → The student wants to learn faster and deeper than the syllabus allows.

In every case, the same idea is at work: one thing is advancing at a greater rate than the other, and that difference is continuous and increasing.

When you use "outpace," you are saying three things at once:

  1. There is a comparison — two things are being measured against each other.
  2. One is faster/greater in rate — not just larger, but growing or moving more rapidly.
  3. This is an ongoing trend — not a one-time moment, but a sustained pattern.

This is why "outpace" is especially powerful in contexts like economics, business, science, and social trends — wherever rates of change matter.

You might wonder: why not just say "faster"?

The word "faster" describes a single moment. "Outpacing" describes a process that continues over time. When something outpaces something else, it means the gap is not static — it is actively widening as time goes on.

For example:

  • "The car is going faster than the bicycle" — a snapshot.
  • "Electric vehicles are outpacing petrol vehicles in sales" — a trend that has been building and continues to build.

This temporal, ongoing quality is what makes "outpace" distinct and precise.
How It Differs from Similar Words

These words are often used similarly, but each has a slightly different flavour:

  • Outrun — more physical, more about literal speed; "he outran the dog."
  • Surpass — about exceeding a level, standard, or achievement; "she surpassed all expectations." (Does not strongly imply rate or speed.)
  • Outstrip — nearly identical to outpace; very common in formal writing. "Outstrip" can refer to degree as well as speed, e.g., "his talent outstripped his peers." Both are widely interchangeable.
  • Exceed — simply go beyond a limit or amount; "costs exceeded the budget." No sense of ongoing rate.

Outpace is the best word when you specifically want to talk about the speed or rate of change of one thing compared to another, especially in a sustained, ongoing way.

"Outpace" sits at a slightly formal register — you'll see it often in:

  • Journalism ("Renewable energy is outpacing fossil fuels in new installations.")
  • Business ("The company's revenue outpaced analyst expectations.")
  • Academic and scientific writing ("Population growth is outpacing food production in the region.")

That said, it is not stiff or difficult — it is widely understood and used across all levels of writing.

The word almost always follows this structure:

[Subject] outpaces [object]

  • Inflation outpaced economic growth.
  • Her ambition outpaced her resources.
  • AI development is outpacing our ability to understand it.

You can also write it in the past ("outpaced"), present continuous ("is outpacing"), or other tenses as needed.
A Simple Test: When to Use "Outpace"

Ask yourself: Is one thing advancing or growing at a faster rate than another, and is this a continuing trend?

If yes → outpace is your word.
One Sentence to Anchor It All

To outpace something means to consistently move, grow, or progress faster than it — so that the gap between the two keeps increasing over time.

Everything else about this word is just this idea applied to different contexts.
